title: The Case for Economic Espionage
gist: Former CIA deputy director David S. Cohen argues the US should formally lift its self-imposed ban on economic espionage and share stolen foreign (chiefly Chinese) trade secrets with US frontier-tech firms, because national security now rides on private-sector dual-use innovation where China is catching up. He proposes an executive order plus Intelligence Authorization Act provisions, NSA-led signals collection, broad intra-sector sharing including startups, and tight congressional oversight to curb favoritism and corruption.

themes.theme: End of the US economic-espionage taboo

insights.claim: The US intelligence community has long barred spying on foreign companies to give US businesses commercial advantage, a norm codified by Obama in PPD-28 in 2014 and reaffirmed by Biden's 2022 executive order, and not publicly rescinded by the second Trump administration.
insights.so_what: A formal policy reversal would be a regime change in how state intelligence interacts with corporate competitiveness.
insights.quote: collecting foreign trade secrets in order to “afford a competitive advantage to U.S. companies” was “not an authorized foreign intelligence or counterintelligence purpose.”
insights.locator: In a 2014 presidential policy directive
insights.speaker: David S. Cohen

insights.claim: David Cohen argues the US should allow intelligence agencies to collect commercial secrets from foreign companies and deliver them to US firms building frontier technologies vital to national security, even if this hands some firms a commercial advantage.
insights.so_what: Signals a possible new state-backed tailwind for US frontier-tech firms competing with China.
insights.quote: Washington needs to rewrite the rules on economic espionage with the explicit aim of helping U.S. frontier firms compete—even if doing so means handing some of them a commercial advantage.

insights.speaker: David S. Cohen

insights.claim: In September 2026 the Trump administration disclosed that the CIA and other agencies had begun broadening espionage against China, including Chinese industry, a de facto step toward economic spying without formally lifting the ban.
insights.so_what: The norm is already eroding informally, raising the odds of formal change and of ad hoc favoritism.

insights.claim: The original rationales for the ban—free-market orthodoxy, government-led innovation, and a US tech lead that meant more to lose than gain—no longer hold because security-critical innovation now comes from private companies and China is contesting or erasing the US lead.
insights.so_what: Structural shift in where national-security value is created reframes policy toward private tech firms.
insights.quote: By abstaining from economic espionage, the United States has tilted the playing field against itself and magnified the Chinese threat.

insights.claim: Obama's 2015 'common understanding' with Xi Jinping against cyber-enabled IP theft and a follow-on G-20 communiqué did not change Chinese behavior; Beijing resumed spying on US industry a few months after a brief lull.
insights.so_what: Diplomatic norms against commercial cyber-theft have proven unenforceable, so unilateral restraint carries real costs.
